summary: A humorous April 1st RFC claiming the IPng working group chose a packet format with 1696 bytes of address space. It is a joke and does not specify anything.

plainLanguage.summary: A joke where each internet address is absurdly long, about 1696 bytes, thousands of times longer than a real one. Don't try this at home.

questions: when was this april fools rfc published
how big is a real ipv6 address
subtitle: An April Fools' joke about absurdly large IP addresses.

tldr.problem: This is an April Fools' RFC: not a serious proposal.
tldr.mechanism: The joke is that the IPng working group decided to use 1696 bytes of address space, making the address field larger than the entire payload, leaving no room for actual data in a packet.
tldr.outcome: The joke highlights a real tension in the IPng (IPv6) design process, where address space debates were ongoing, while poking fun at priorities. The 1696-byte figure is divisible by 53 (ATM cell size), and the joke suggests this was intentional.

today: RFC 1776 is an April Fools' RFC: a humorous document that does not propose anything real. IPv6, actually standardized in 1998, uses 128-bit (16-byte) addresses. This joke document remains a memorable example of RFC humor and the intensity of the addressing debates in the 1990s.

sections.title: The Joke
sections.content:
This RFC, published on April 1, 1995, is a humorous document written by Steve Crocker. It announces that the IPng working group has chosen a packet format with 1696 bytes devoted to addressing. This means almost all of a packet is address information and almost no space remains for data.

The punchline is captured in the title: "The Address is the Message." Crocker sardonically notes that by focusing so heavily on addressing, the working group has solved the confidentiality and integrity problems of Internet security by eliminating the content of the message entirely.
sections.plainLanguage: Steve Crocker jokes that the IPng team picked addresses so big you could not fit any actual data in a packet. The joke is funny because by then, addresses were taking up a lot of engineering energy.

sections.title: The Context
sections.content:
In the mid-1990s, the Internet Engineering Task Force was designing IPv6 (then called IPng, for "IP next generation") to address the impending exhaustion of IPv4 addresses. The working group debated address space requirements extensively.

Crocker's joke targets the intensity of these debates by proposing an absurd resolution: use 1696 bytes—more than thirty times larger than an IPv6 address. The 1696-byte figure is divisible by 53, the size of an ATM cell, which was another technology under consideration at the time.
sections.plainLanguage: Back then, people were arguing about how big Internet addresses should be for the next generation of the Internet. Crocker jokes that the argument got so intense they picked a silly size.

sections.title: The Punchline
sections.content:
Security experts in the joke "hail this as a major breakthrough" because with no data, there are no confidentiality or integrity problems. Law enforcement and intelligence agencies are "silently thankful" they can focus on detecting who talks to whom instead of debating key escrow and export control—issues that were genuinely contentious at the time.

Service providers immediately start competing for reserved portions of this massive address space, a cynical nod to how organizations often claimed large address allocations regardless of actual need.
sections.plainLanguage: If your message has no content, nobody can read your secrets, and spies just watch who calls whom. Companies immediately fight to claim pieces of this huge address space, even though they do not need it.
